report.source_text: A 22-year-old male patient reported swelling without pain on the right side of his face since childhood as the chief complaint. On further interrogation, the patient said that the swelling had been growing gradually over the years and has now become of the present size, which was approximately fist-sized. The patient did not recall any history of trauma. The extraoral examination demonstrated a swelling on the face's right side, extending supero-inferiorly from the right eye's outer canthus to the mandible's lower border and anteroposteriorly from the right corner of the mouth to the pre-tragus region (Figure 1). The painless swelling was fluctuant, compressible, and soft in consistency on palpation. There was a slight rise in temperature over the surface of the swelling. On temporomandibular joint examination, the deviation was present towards the left side while closing the jaw without any pain, crepitus, or clicking sound. Intra-oral examination revealed bluish-red discolouration in the posterior part of the right side buccal mucosa extending up to the right side soft palatal region (Figure 2). Maxillo-mandibular bony morphology was within the standard limit in the vicinity of the swelling. On bimanual palpation, the lesion was soft and compressible, non-tender, and had a diffuse periphery with evident pulsation. While palpating, the lesion was exaggerated, and an elevated red-purplish lesion appeared in the posterior part of the mucosa (Figure 3). All the teeth were in good condition. Only extrinsic stains and calculus were there. Panoramic and submentovertex radiographs showed the presence of multiple concentric calcifications in the soft tissue shadow of the lesion suggestive of phleboliths (Figures 4, 5). Assuring the benign nature of the disease and possible definite treatment, the patient was referred to the department of interventional radiology for management.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 22-year-old male presented with a lifelong, painless, fluctuating, and compressible swelling on the right side of his face with a bluish-red, pulsatile intraoral lesion. Physical exam revealed swelling extending from the outer canthus to the mandible and from the mouth corner to the pre-tragus region, fluctuant and slightly warm. Intraoral exam showed bluish-red discoloration and an elevated red-purplish lesion with pulsation. Panoramic and submentovertex radiographs revealed multiple concentric calcifications suggestive of phleboliths, supporting vascular malformation diagnosis. The patient was referred to interventional radiology for management. These findings are consistent with a hemangioma diagnosis based on typical clinical and radiographic features.
